content: The following individuals and groups have been identified as effective in encouraging men to undergo Voluntary Medical Male Circumcision (VMMC): family members, sexual partners in committed relationships, peers and friends (especially satisfied VMMC clients), cultural, traditional, and religious leaders, as well as celebrities, ambassadors, and other role models. Differentiated service delivery and innovative demand creation strategies have significantly increased the uptake of VMMC services. During the intervention period, the majority of clients belonged to the priority age group of 15–34 years. Among the districts, eThekwini and Zululand outperformed others in mobilizing adult men for VMMC, with over 50% of men aged 15–34 years reached. From October 2015 to September 2018, the number of VMMCs performed in eThekwini increased from 10,774 to 50,042, while in Zululand, the numbers rose from 9,922 to 21,833. Key lessons learned include: 1. Collaboration with government initiatives and traditional leadership is critical for success. 2. Employing social mobilizers from the communities they serve is highly effective. 3. Demand creation efforts must be tailored to the local context. 4. Conducting mobilization activities in locations frequented by men, such as barbershops and taverns, is particularly impactful. 5. Promoting the comprehensive benefits of VMMC, beyond just HIV prevention, has proven effective in engaging adult men. In Tanzania, embedding VMMC services within community-based HIV testing services (HTS) has been successful in increasing uptake among older men. Challenges included low national coverage of the 25–29-year-old target group and barriers such as distance to services, long waiting times, and lack of privacy. To address these issues, the AIDSFree project collaborated with the Sauti project to integrate VMMC services into mobile HTS teams. This included embedding a team of VMMC providers within the HTS teams to offer same-day circumcision services. Tents were set up near hotspots, and clients were asked about their circumcision status during HTS. Those uncircumcised were offered on-site VMMC services or referred to nearby facilities. Results showed that prior to full implementation, older men accounted for only 3% of all VMMCs performed. This increased to 5% in the fourth quarter of 2018. Mobile services were particularly effective, with older men comprising 38% of clients served through this modality, compared to 11% through routine services. Key lessons learned include: 1. Mobile VMMC services are better suited to overcoming barriers such as distance, waiting times, and privacy concerns. 2. Female providers, even if non-local, do not deter older men from accessing services and may reduce embarrassment. 3. Collaboration between HTS targeting key populations and VMMC services can maximize uptake among older men. In Zimbabwe, soccer galas were used as a demand creation strategy to increase VMMC uptake among males aged 15–29 years. Challenges included cultural and religious perceptions that VMMC was for young boys and reluctance among older boys and men to visit service delivery points. The initiative involved engaging community leaders, soccer teams, and schools to gain buy-in. Services were delivered at nearby clinics and mobile caravans stationed at sports fields. Soccer matches were held, with winners receiving prizes, and additional services such as cervical cancer screening and HIV testing were offered. Results included: 187 clients circumcised, with 91% in the target age group of 15–29 years. 34 women screened for cervical cancer. Over 250 clients tested for HIV. Key lessons learned include: 1. Community involvement facilitates reaching and convincing men and boys to undergo circumcision. 2. Allowing communities to take ownership of programs increases their effectiveness. 3. Using soccer as an engagement tool helps attract large audiences and increases service uptake. 4. Integrating related services in one location benefits entire families and enhances health outcomes. In Mberengwa, Zimbabwe, efforts were made to incorporate VMMC into traditional circumcision practices among the VaRemba tribe. Challenges included adverse events due to poor hygiene, lack of documentation, and absence of clear protocols for consent, counseling, and follow-up.
